title: Evaluation Metrics — Classification
summary: Read a confusion matrix correctly and pick the metric that actually matches the business cost of being wrong.

slides.subTitle: The confusion matrix
slides.markdown:
Every binary classifier's output on a labeled set boils down to four counts. **True positive (TP)** — predicted positive, actually positive. **False positive (FP)** — predicted positive, actually negative (a false alarm). **True negative (TN)** — predicted negative, actually negative. **False negative (FN)** — predicted negative, actually positive (a miss).

Every classification metric — accuracy, precision, recall, F1 — is just arithmetic on these four numbers. Get comfortable reading a confusion matrix and every downstream metric becomes obvious rather than memorized.

slides.subTitle: Why accuracy lies
slides.markdown:
**Accuracy** = (TP + TN) / total — the fraction you got right. It's intuitive, and wrong for imbalanced data. In fraud detection where 1 in 1,000 transactions is fraudulent, a model that predicts "not fraud" every single time scores **99.9% accuracy** while catching zero fraud.

Accuracy treats every class as equally important and equally common — neither is true in most real classification problems. Whenever one class is rare or errors carry different costs, accuracy stops being the metric that matters.

slides.subTitle: The trade-off
slides.markdown:
**Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — of everything you flagged positive, how much was actually positive. It protects against **false alarms**. **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN) — of everything actually positive, how much did you catch. It protects against **misses**.

They trade off: flag more aggressively and recall rises but precision falls; flag conservatively and precision rises but recall falls. A spam filter favors precision (don't bury real email); a cancer screen favors recall (don't miss a case).

slides.subTitle: F1 and F-beta
slides.markdown:
**F1** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall — it only scores high when *both* are reasonably high, unlike a plain average that lets one compensate for the other. **F-beta** generalizes it with a weight: **F2** weights recall twice as important as precision (good for cancer screening, where misses are costlier); **F0.5** weights precision higher (good for spam filtering, where false alarms are costlier).

Pick beta from the actual cost ratio of a miss versus a false alarm — don't default to F1 out of habit.

slides.subTitle: ROC and AUC
slides.markdown:
The **ROC curve** plots **TPR** against **FPR** across every threshold. A random classifier traces the diagonal; a perfect one hugs the top-left corner. **AUC** condenses it to one number — the probability a random positive scores higher than a random negative. 0.5 is guessing; 1.0 is perfect.

slides.subTitle: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
slides.markdown:
Both summarize a classifier across all thresholds, but they disagree badly on rare-positive data.

| | ROC-AUC | PR-AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Axes | TPR vs FPR | Precision vs recall |
| Uses TN count | Yes (via FPR) | No |
| On rare positives | Stays high, hides poor precision | Drops, exposes it |
| Best for | Balanced classes | Imbalanced, rare positive class |

With 1% positives, a huge TN count keeps FPR tiny even when FP is large relative to TP — ROC-AUC looks great while precision is terrible. PR-AUC ignores TN entirely, so it reflects that pain directly. Fraud, disease screening, and rare-event detection should report PR-AUC first.

slides.subTitle: Setting the threshold from cost
slides.markdown:
A classifier outputs a probability; you choose the **threshold** that turns it into a decision — 0.5 is a default, not a rule. Set it from the real cost of each error. If a missed fraud case costs $500 and a false alarm costs $2 in support time, you should tolerate many more false alarms to catch more fraud — lower the threshold.

Compute expected cost = FP_count × cost(FP) + FN_count × cost(FN) across candidate thresholds on a validation set, and pick the minimum. The "best" threshold is a business decision expressed in the model's units, not a statistics default.

slides.subTitle: The 99% accuracy trap
slides.markdown:
A model reports 99% accuracy on a dataset where only 1% of examples are positive (fraud, disease, defect). It sounds like a win — but a model that predicts the negative class every single time hits that same 99% while catching **zero** positives. The metric rewarded doing nothing.

Before trusting an accuracy number, check the class balance. On imbalanced data, report **precision, recall, and PR-AUC** instead — they can't be gamed by predicting the majority class, and they surface exactly how many real positives you're actually catching.

Precision, recall, and F1 are defined per class, so a multi-class problem needs a way to combine them into one number. **Macro-average** computes the metric per class and averages them **unweighted** — every class counts equally regardless of how common it is. **Weighted-average** weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has, so common classes dominate the score.

The choice changes the story: on a 10-class problem where one rare class (2% of data) is always misclassified, macro-average tanks visibly (that class's 0% recall pulls the average down hard), while weighted-average barely moves, since that class is a tiny share of the weighting. Pick macro when every class matters regardless of frequency (rare disease subtypes); pick weighted when overall performance on the actual traffic mix is what matters.
